To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) The standard renewal equation theory can be applied to a timeindependent age-structured population model with harvesting; (ii) the standard theory is not valid for the time-dependent model, but the standard theory is a good approximation if the harvesting season is short; (iii) for a given harvesting policy, a population can be made to grow or decline by changing the age of the oldest individuals that are harvested; (iv) the standard theory does not predict the correct long-term population growth

(a) The population grows at a rate that depends on the birth rate, the death rate, and the harvesting policy; (b) The growth rate of the population is bounded above by the birth rate and below by the death rate; and (c) The growth rate can be approximated by a function of the birth rate, death rate, and harvesting policy.

the optimal harvest rate is a function of the population age distribution and is not the same for all age distributions; the optimal harvest rate depends on the season of the year, and the optimal harvesting policy is to harvest the population of all ages for a given fraction of the year and then to stop harvesting for the rest of the year.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of models for the management of renewable resources, and the analysis of these models in order to determine optimal policies.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the harvesting policy is not optimal in the sense that it does not maximize the long term average population size, but it does provide a reasonable tradeoff between population size and the fraction of the population harvested.
the harvesting policy should be applied to a population of older age, but the exact age will depend on the age structure of the population.
the population growth is slowed down by harvesting, and this effect is most pronounced when the harvest is done on the young.
